content.title: About
content.content: Venison is lean meat from a deer, typically taken from the loin or other premium cuts. A venison steak is known for its tender texture, slightly sweet aroma, and low fat content compared with beef. It is commonly grilled, pan‑seared, or roasted and served with sauces and side dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Venison is one of the most diet‑friendly meats, providing about 120 kcal per 100 g.
The meat is rich in heme iron, making it an excellent source of readily absorbable iron.
In the wild, deer feed on grasses, leaves, and berries, which influence the subtle flavor of their meat.
Venison has a long culinary tradition in Scandinavia, Russia, and North America.
Dry‑aging venison steaks can enhance tenderness and develop deeper flavor notes.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Venison contains less saturated fat than beef, making it suitable for low‑fat dietary plans.

items.title: High‑quality protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 22 g of complete protein essential for muscle growth and repair.

items.title: Rich in iron
items.content: The iron in venison is highly bioavailable, helping to prevent anemia.

items.title: Source of zinc and selenium
items.content: These trace minerals support immune function and antioxidant protection.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Venison supplies vitamin B12, niacin, and riboflavin, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Meat allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to venison, manifested as skin rashes or gastrointestinal symptoms.

items.title: Possible parasites
items.content: Raw or undercooked venison can harbor parasites; thorough cooking is recommended.

items.title: High purine content
items.content: Venison is rich in purines, which may be problematic for people with gout or uric acid metabolism disorders.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Venison steak is best cooked quickly over high heat—grill, broiler, or hot pan—to retain juiciness. Marinating in olive oil with rosemary, garlic, and black pepper enhances flavor. Serve with butter‑based sauces, berry chutney, or a vegetable side.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh venison refrigerated at 0‑2 °C in a sealed bag for 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze at –18 °C; it retains quality for up to 6 months. Thaw in the refrigerator rather than at room temperature.
